振音拍屬體鳴樂器（112.1），發聲時一手握金屬線，另一手掌心敲擊木球；箱內鬆動: The vibraslap is an idiophone (112.1): one hand holds the metal rod and the other strikes the wooden ball with the palm; the loose metal pins or rivets inside the box vibrate and knock against the wooden box, producing a rattle and a knock. The wooden box acts as the resonator, so that the sound of the metal parts inside comes out through the box. The source gives no range and no way of controlling the volume. Compared with the traditional donkey's or zebra's jawbone, it replaces the loose teeth with a wooden ball, a metal rod and metal pins in a box, and it is the modern version, which does not break easily.
振音拍屬體鳴樂器，北美現代版本，由一根彎成U形的硬金屬線連接木製球體與中空木盒；: The vibraslap is an idiophone; in its modern North American version a hard metal rod bent into a U joins a wooden ball to a hollow wooden box. Inside the box are metal teeth and a metal mechanism fixed with loose pins or rivets, and when the ball is struck the metal parts vibrate and knock inside the box. It comes in various sizes and materials, and the sources do not state the particular woods, the metals or the reed material of each part.
振音拍為北美體鳴打擊樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號112.1，可聽見: The vibraslap is a North American percussion idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.1, to be heard on the 1967 US number-one single "Green Tambourine" (Lemon Pipers); in the recording of "Sweet Emotion", Steven Tyler broke it on the third use and the crack stayed in the recording; Tally Hall also often use one on stage, named Henry. Its predecessor goes back to the African jawbone, which came to South America with enslaved people and is called quijada. It sounds when the wooden ball is struck and the metal teeth inside the box vibrate.
振音拍的歷史可追溯至非洲的下顎骨樂器，以驢或斑馬的下顎骨敲擊，鬆動牙齒震動發聲；: The vibraslap's history goes back to the African jawbone instrument, struck on a donkey's or zebra's jawbone so that the loose teeth vibrate; it came to South America with enslaved people and is called quijada. In 1967 Martin Cohen took out the first patent, turning the animal-skull idea into the modern version with a metal rod, a wooden ball and metal pins in a wooden box. The percussionist Bobby Rosengarden had suggested making a jawbone that would not break easily, and Cohen also mentions having heard such a sound on a Cal Tjader album.

The vibraslap is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.1, marked as belonging to the Americas / North America and descended from the African "jawbone" tradition, of which it is the modern version. A horseshoe-shaped hard metal rod joins a wooden ball to a hollow wooden box containing metal teeth or loose pins; the player holds the rod in one hand and strikes the ball against the palm of the other, so that the metal mechanism inside the box vibrates, knocks and sounds. It is used by percussionists and appears in recordings and live performance.
演奏者一手握住振音拍的金屬線，另一手以掌心作為敲擊面，將木球敲向掌心。箱體為共鳴: The player holds the metal rod of the vibraslap in one hand and uses the other palm as the striking surface, knocking the wooden ball against it. The box is the resonator; inside it are loose metal pins or rivets, and after the stroke these vibrate and knock against the walls of the box, making the rattle. A beginner can first practise holding the rod steady, then bring the ball against the palm with a light, definite movement, taking care not to strike the box itself, which would spoil the resonance and the tone.
